title: Iran says it struck US radar in Bahrain as kingdom issues first threat alerts since September
dek: Blasts and sirens were reported across Bahrain before dawn on Sunday as Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed a six-drone strike, the second in three days. The US says it shot down the drones fired on Friday; India, with a large community in the Gulf, is watching the fragile lull.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Sunday that it had attacked a US air-defence radar at a base in Bahrain with six drones, as blasts and sirens were heard across the island kingdom before dawn and its government issued its first public threat alerts since September. It was the second such claim in three days, and it tests a lull in direct US-Iran fighting that had held for weeks.

The US military said it had shot down the two drones Iran launched towards Bahrain on Friday, with no injuries or damage. Bahrain said later on Sunday that its air defences had intercepted the attacks, and neither Washington nor Manama had reported any damage by Sunday evening India time. The IRGC's claims could not be independently verified.

## What happened

Explosions were heard in Bahrain at about 4 am local time on Sunday (6.30 am IST), and residents reported a second series of blasts at about 6.30 am (9 am IST), according to reports from Manama. Bahrain's interior ministry issued two alerts within a little over two hours, urging residents in a post on X to "remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location" and to follow official channels. It did not say where the threat came from. Bahrain's state television said early on Sunday that the country's air defences had intercepted and destroyed an Iranian drone, according to reports.

In a statement carried by Iran's state broadcaster, the IRGC said the radar at the Al-Riffa helicopter base had been "targeted by six drones belonging to the IRGC Aerospace Force". It called the strike the "second phase" of its response to what it described as hostile US actions. The statement also said: "The Strait of Hormuz is closed," and warned that "any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response."

The first phase came on Friday, when the IRGC said it had hit a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in retaliation for what it said was a US strike on a telecommunications tower in Sirik, in Iran's Hormozgan province. US Central Command (CENTCOM) rejected that account in a post on X: "The IRGC launched two one-way attack drones toward Bahrain and both were shot down by U.S. forces. There were no injuries or damage." It did not address the allegation about the tower. Friday's claim was the first Iranian claim of an attack on US military assets in a Gulf state since early September, according to reports.

## Bahrain: "a resumption of Iran's aggression"

Later on Sunday Bahrain's military said its air defences had intercepted several Iranian "aerial attacks" on Riffa Air Base, which is used by US forces, according to reports. It did not report damage or casualties. Bahrain's foreign ministry condemned what it called "a resumption of Iran's aggression", said the attacks violated international law and that "no pretext can legitimise violations of state sovereignty", and said Bahrain rejected the use of its territory "to settle accounts" and held Iran fully responsible, according to reports.

Iran's foreign ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, said the role of regional countries in helping the US attack Iran had been "documented". He said Iran's strikes were justified under Article 51 of the UN Charter, which covers self-defence, and were "purely defensive in nature", aimed only at US bases and assets used against Iran, according to reports. Jordan condemned the attacks as a violation of Bahrain's sovereignty, and Egypt said it rejected attacks that threatened regional stability and that Bahrain's security was linked to its own, reports said.

The IRGC also claimed on Saturday that it had shot down a US MQ-1 drone over Qeshm Island, which it said was the 17th. The US has not confirmed any such loss.

On another front, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Sunday that it had intercepted two Houthi ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh and three drones over Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province, according to reports. The Houthis and the coalition have exchanged attacks all week, including Houthi claims, which Saudi Arabia has not confirmed, of strikes on its main oil export routes.

## Background

The war began on 28 February, when the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran. Iran has since struck airports, seaports, energy facilities and US bases across the Gulf. Bahrain, which hosts the headquarters of the US Navy's Fifth Fleet, has been among the countries hit hardest. Its airspace was closed on 28 February, and in March the Indian embassy in Manama issued an advisory and a 24-hour helpline, 00973-39418071, and arranged for stranded Indians to leave through Saudi Arabia.

Iran has kept shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel between Iran and Oman that carries a large share of the world's seaborne oil and gas, heavily restricted. The US Navy says it has escorted more than 1.5 billion barrels of Gulf crude through the strait since June, and the US has kept up a naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The past week has sent mixed signals. On Thursday, President Donald Trump wrote on social media: "We don't need a deal with Iran." On Saturday, people familiar with his discussions said he had told advisers he might hold off on new attacks on Iran unless there were fresh provocations from Tehran or the Houthis, while keeping the blockade in place, according to reports. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan had urged him not to resume strikes, the reports said; he made no commitment. A White House official said only the President knew what he would do, and when.

Oil markets had been calming. In its monthly oil market report on Friday, the International Energy Agency said the world market was returning to surplus for the first time since the war began, as Gulf exports recovered: it put supply in the last three months of 2026 at about 105 million barrels a day, roughly 1.7 million barrels a day above demand. It said tight diesel supply remained the "overriding concern". Brent crude had climbed back towards $96 a barrel on Friday after the Houthi claims.

## Why it matters for India

India imports most of its crude oil, and much of it, along with liquefied natural gas and cooking gas, has traditionally come through Hormuz. Any renewed fighting in the Gulf pushes up the cost of fuel and freight, and the rupee has already weakened past 94 to the dollar this month as oil prices rose. Bahrain and its neighbours are also home to a large Indian community whose safety and remittances are directly exposed to attacks on Gulf states.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi said this week that the government had absorbed Rs 43 a litre of diesel costs to shield farmers from the oil shock. A fresh round of Gulf attacks would make that harder to sustain.

## What they are saying

The IRGC, in its statement: "Any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response."

CENTCOM, on Friday's attack: "There were no injuries or damage."

Bahrain's interior ministry, to residents: "Remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location."

Bahrain's foreign ministry: "No pretext can legitimise violations of state sovereignty."

Iran's foreign ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei: the strikes were "purely defensive in nature".

## What happens next

Mr Trump is due in Manila on Tuesday for meetings with Southeast Asian leaders, and is expected to meet China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, where a three-way meeting with Russia's Vladimir Putin is also planned. Energy security, including fuel-sharing schemes in response to the Gulf crisis, is on the agenda of the ASEAN summit that opened in Manila on Sunday. The IEA's next oil market report is due on 11 December.

## Timeline

- 28 February: US and Israeli strikes on Iran begin the war; Bahrain's airspace closes.
- Early September: last Iranian claim of an attack on US assets in a Gulf state before this week.
- 12 November: Mr Trump says the US does not need a deal with Iran.
- 13 November: IRGC claims strike on US radar in Bahrain; CENTCOM says it shot down two drones.
- 14 November: reports say Mr Trump may hold off on new attacks barring provocations.
- 15 November: IRGC claims six-drone attack on Al-Riffa base; Bahrain issues alerts, says it intercepted the attacks and accuses Iran of "aggression".
